subject: biology

items.q: Enzymes catalyse specific reactions. What causes this specificity?
items.correct: The shape of the enzyme's active site.
items.misconception: The temperature at which the enzyme works.
items.why: Students apply the rule they learn for ordinary chemical reactions, where heating increases the rate, without allowing for the shape of the active site. Students should be able to relate enzyme activity to temperature changes: above the optimum the active site changes shape, so the rate falls.
items.random_wrong: The amount of the enzyme that is used.

items.q: Which statement describes the lock and key theory of enzyme action?
items.correct: The substrate fits the enzyme's active site.
items.misconception: The enzyme fits into every kind of substrate.
items.why: Students think of enzymes as a general 'food-breaking' chemical rather than as molecules with a particular shape. Enzymes catalyse specific reactions in living organisms due to the shape of their active site, so only one type of substrate fits.
items.random_wrong: The enzyme is used up by its own substrate.

items.q: An enzyme-controlled reaction is fastest at 40 degrees Celsius. What happens at 60 degrees Celsius?
items.correct: The rate falls because the active site changes shape.
items.misconception: The rate falls because the enzyme has been killed.
items.why: The word 'kill' is used for microorganisms harmed by heat, and students transfer it to enzymes because enzymes are made by living cells. Enzymes are protein molecules. Above the optimum temperature the shape of the active site changes, so the substrate no longer fits and the reaction stops.
items.random_wrong: The rate falls because the enzyme is used up.

items.q: Protease in the stomach works fastest at pH 2. What happens to its activity at pH 8?
items.correct: It falls, as the active site changes shape.
items.misconception: It rises, as enzymes work best at about pH 7.
items.why: Neutral pH is treated as 'normal' in chemistry lessons, so students assume every enzyme in the body must need it. Students should be able to relate enzyme activity to pH changes: protease in the stomach works in acid conditions, while enzymes in the small intestine work in alkaline conditions.
items.random_wrong: It falls, as the enzyme is killed by alkali.

items.q: Amylase broke down 20 mg of starch in 5 minutes. What was the mean rate of reaction?
items.correct: 4 mg per minute
items.misconception: 0.25 mg per minute
items.why: Students recall that rate involves a division but not which quantity goes on top. Students should be able to carry out rate calculations for chemical reactions: rate is the amount changed per unit of time.
items.random_wrong: 20 mg per minute

items.q: Enzymes are involved in metabolism. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: Enzymes catalyse the reactions of metabolism in cells.
items.misconception: Enzymes give the reactions the energy that they need.
items.why: Students link enzymes with speed and speed with energy, so they treat the enzyme as a source of energy. Enzymes are catalysts that catalyse specific reactions in living organisms due to the shape of their active site.
items.random_wrong: Enzymes are used up in the reactions that they speed up.

items.q: Which statement about digestive enzymes is correct?
items.correct: Protease is made in the stomach and pancreas.
items.misconception: Bile is the enzyme that breaks down fat droplets.
items.why: Bile acts on fat and is released into the small intestine with the digestive enzymes, so students group it with them. Bile emulsifies fat to form small droplets which increases the surface area, and the alkaline conditions and large surface area increase the rate of fat breakdown by lipase.
items.random_wrong: One enzyme is able to digest every type of food.

items.q: What does lipase break lipids down into?
items.correct: Glycerol and fatty acids
items.misconception: Glucose and fatty acids
items.why: Glucose is the product students meet most often, because of respiration, so it becomes the default answer for every food group. Carbohydrases break down carbohydrates to simple sugars, proteases break down proteins to amino acids, and lipases break down lipids (fats) to glycerol and fatty acids.
items.random_wrong: Amino acids and simple sugars

items.q: Why does bile increase the rate of fat breakdown by lipase?
items.correct: It emulsifies fat, so surface area increases.
items.misconception: It digests the fat into fatty acids and glycerol.
items.why: Bile acts on fat and is released into the small intestine with the digestive enzymes, so students group it with them. Bile emulsifies fat to form small droplets which increases the surface area, and the alkaline conditions and large surface area increase the rate of fat breakdown by lipase.
items.random_wrong: It gives the lipase the energy that it needs.

items.q: What happens to the products of digestion after they are absorbed?
items.correct: They build new carbohydrates, lipids and proteins.
items.misconception: Every product is turned into glucose and stored.
items.why: Glucose is the product students meet most often, because of respiration, so it becomes the default answer for every food group. Carbohydrases break down carbohydrates to simple sugars, proteases break down proteins to amino acids, and lipases break down lipids (fats) to glycerol and fatty acids.
items.random_wrong: They are all used in respiration to give energy.

items.q: Which statement about the double circulatory system is correct?
items.correct: The right ventricle pumps blood to the lungs.
items.misconception: Blood passes through the heart once each circuit.
items.why: Students picture the circulation as a single loop, which is what a diagram of one artery and one vein suggests. The heart pumps blood around the body in a double circulatory system.
items.random_wrong: Arteries carry blood with oxygen to the lungs.

items.q: Which feature of the alveoli increases the rate of gaseous exchange?
items.correct: A large surface area and a good blood supply.
items.misconception: A wide tube that carries air down to the lungs.
items.why: The trachea and bronchi are the largest and most obvious structures on a diagram, so students assume the important work happens there. Knowledge of the lungs is restricted to the trachea, bronchi, alveoli and the capillary network surrounding the alveoli; the alveoli are where gaseous exchange occurs.
items.random_wrong: A thick outer wall that resists air pressure.

items.q: Which pairing of a blood vessel with its structure is correct?
items.correct: Artery: thick wall resists the high pressure.
items.misconception: Vein: thick muscular wall resists high pressure.
items.why: Veins look wide and obvious under the skin, so students assume they must be strongly built. Students should be able to explain how the structure of the vessels relates to their functions: an artery has a thick wall to withstand high pressure, while a vein has a thin wall and valves.
items.random_wrong: Capillary: thick wall resists the blood pressure.

items.q: A heart pumps 300 cm3 of blood in 4 seconds. What is the rate of blood flow?
items.correct: 75 cm3 per second
items.misconception: 1200 cm3 per second
items.why: Students see two numbers in a rate question and combine them with the operation that gives the larger, more impressive answer. Students should be able to carry out rate calculations for chemical reactions: divide the amount changed by the time taken.
items.random_wrong: 300 cm3 per second

items.q: A photograph shows the cells in a sample of blood. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: Red blood cells have no nucleus, so they carry more oxygen.
items.misconception: Platelets move around the blood and destroy pathogens.
items.why: Platelets are small fragments that look like cells in a photograph, so students confuse them with white blood cells. Blood consists of plasma, in which the red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets are suspended: white blood cells defend against pathogens and platelets help clotting.
items.random_wrong: Plasma is the liquid that carries oxygen to the cells.

items.q: Which statement about the treatment of coronary heart disease is correct?
items.correct: Stents are used to keep the coronary arteries open.
items.misconception: Statins are used to widen the blocked coronary arteries.
items.why: Statins and stents are taught together as treatments for the same disease and their names sound alike. Stents are used to keep the coronary arteries open. Statins are widely used to reduce blood cholesterol levels, which slows down the rate of fatty material deposit.
items.random_wrong: Stents are used to lower the level of blood cholesterol.

items.q: A person has a heart valve that has developed a leak. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: Blood flows backwards through the leaking valve.
items.misconception: The volume of blood pumped stays the same.
items.why: The heart keeps beating and the person often feels well at first, so students assume nothing has changed. In some people heart valves may become faulty, preventing the valve from opening fully, or the heart valve might develop a leak; students should understand the consequences of faulty valves.
items.random_wrong: Only a heart transplant can treat the problem.

items.q: Why might an artificial heart be used for a patient with heart failure?
items.correct: It keeps a patient alive while awaiting a donor.
items.misconception: It replaces a faulty valve inside the patient.
items.why: Valves are part of the heart, so students assume the whole organ has to be replaced. Faulty heart valves can be replaced using biological or mechanical valves; a donor heart is transplanted in the case of heart failure.
items.random_wrong: It cures the heart failure without any further care.

items.q: Which statement best describes health?
items.correct: The state of both physical and mental well-being.
items.misconception: The state of being free of catching diseases.
items.why: Diseases are taught in separate categories, so students treat communicable disease, cancer, allergy and mental illness as unconnected. Different types of disease may interact: defects in the immune system mean an individual is more likely to suffer from infectious diseases, viruses living in cells can be the trigger for cancers, immune reactions initially caused by a pathogen can trigger allergies, and severe physical ill health can lead to depression and other mental illness.
items.random_wrong: The state of having no risk factors present.

items.q: Which statement about the interaction of different types of disease is correct?
items.correct: An immune reaction to a pathogen can trigger allergies.
items.misconception: Communicable disease has no effect on other illness.
items.why: Diseases are taught in separate categories, so students treat communicable disease, cancer, allergy and mental illness as unconnected. Different types of disease may interact: defects in the immune system mean an individual is more likely to suffer from infectious diseases, viruses living in cells can be the trigger for cancers, immune reactions initially caused by a pathogen can trigger allergies, and severe physical ill health can lead to depression and other mental illness.
items.random_wrong: Mental illness is not affected by physical illness.

items.q: A scatter diagram shows a correlation between hours of exercise and heart health. What can be concluded?
items.correct: The variables are linked, but no cause is proven.
items.misconception: Exercise has been proved to cause good heart health.
items.why: Graphs feel like proof, and students are taught to describe a pattern before they are taught what a pattern can and cannot show. A causal mechanism has been proven for some risk factors, but not in others; students should use a scatter diagram to identify a correlation between two variables.
items.random_wrong: People who exercise avoid getting heart disease.

items.q: A scientist studies whether a substance is a risk factor using data from 20 people. Why is this a problem?
items.correct: The sample is too small to be representative.
items.misconception: A risk factor affects each person in the sample.
items.why: The word 'factor' sounds like a cause, and students know one person who was affected, so they read a population statement as a personal certainty. Risk factors are linked to an increased rate of a disease, and many diseases are caused by the interaction of a number of factors.
items.random_wrong: The sample size has no effect on the result.

items.q: Smoking is described as a risk factor for lung cancer. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: It is a factor linked to an increased rate of disease.
items.misconception: A correlation in data proves that it is a cause.
items.why: Graphs feel like proof, and students are taught to describe a pattern before they are taught what a pattern can and cannot show. A causal mechanism has been proven for some risk factors, but not in others; students should use a scatter diagram to identify a correlation between two variables.
items.random_wrong: It is the one risk factor for this type of cancer.

items.q: What is happening to the cells in a tumour?
items.correct: Changes in cells lead to uncontrolled growth.
items.misconception: The cells in the tissue die and are not replaced.
items.why: Cancer is associated with damage and death, so students assume the cells themselves are dying. Cancer is the result of changes in cells that lead to uncontrolled growth and division.
items.random_wrong: Benign cells travel around in the bloodstream.

items.q: How do malignant tumour cells differ from benign tumour cells?
items.correct: They invade tissues and form secondary tumours.
items.misconception: They stay inside a membrane in one part of the body.
items.why: Any tumour sounds dangerous, so students treat 'benign' and 'malignant' as two words for the same thing. Benign tumours are growths of abnormal cells which are contained in one area, usually within a membrane, and they do not invade other parts of the body.
items.random_wrong: They are caused by lifestyle rather than by genes.

items.q: What happens to an enzyme molecule after it has catalysed a reaction?
items.correct: It is unchanged, so it can catalyse the same reaction again.
items.misconception: Enzymes are used up in the reactions they catalyse.
items.why: Students see the substrate disappear during a reaction and assume the enzyme is consumed with it, as a reactant would be. Enzymes catalyse specific reactions in living organisms due to the shape of their active site; the enzyme is not changed by the reaction, so a small amount can keep working.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In the lock and key theory, what fits into what?
items.correct: The substrate fits into the active site of the enzyme.
items.misconception: The enzyme changes its shape so that it fits whatever substrate is present.
items.why: Students remember that shape matters but not which molecule is fixed, and 'key' and 'lock' get swapped. In the lock and key theory, used as a simplified model to explain enzyme action, the active site is the lock and the substrate is the key that fits it.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Where are digestive enzymes produced?
items.correct: In several organs, including the salivary glands, the stomach, the pancreas and the small intestine.
items.misconception: All digestive enzymes are made in the stomach.
items.why: The stomach is the organ students most associate with digestion, so they assume it is where all the chemistry happens. Students should be able to recall the sites of production of amylase, proteases and lipases, which include the salivary glands, stomach, pancreas and small intestine.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which organ makes bile?
items.correct: The liver makes bile; the gall bladder stores it.
items.misconception: Bile is made in the gall bladder.
items.why: The gall bladder is the organ bile is released from, and its name is the one students meet alongside bile. Bile is made in the liver and stored in the gall bladder.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does metabolism mean breaking substances down?
items.correct: No. Metabolism includes reactions that build molecules up as well as reactions that break them down.
items.misconception: Metabolism means only the breaking down of substances, such as the digestion of food.
items.why: Students meet enzymes first in digestion, where large molecules are broken down, and generalise from that example. Metabolism is the sum of all the reactions in a cell or the body, and the products of digestion are used to build new carbohydrates, lipids and proteins.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are all the products of digestion used for energy?
items.correct: No. They are used to build new molecules; only some glucose is used in respiration.
items.misconception: All the products of digestion are used in respiration to release energy.
items.why: Food is described in everyday language as 'fuel', so students assume every digested molecule is burned. The products of digestion are used to build new carbohydrates, lipids and proteins. Some glucose is used in respiration.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is digestion just the breaking of food into smaller pieces?
items.correct: No. Digestive enzymes change large insoluble molecules into different, smaller soluble molecules.
items.misconception: Digestion simply breaks food into smaller pieces of the same substance.
items.why: Chewing and the emulsification of fat are physical changes, so students assume the whole process is physical. Digestive enzymes convert food into small soluble molecules that can be absorbed into the bloodstream, such as simple sugars, amino acids, glycerol and fatty acids.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the rate of blood flow the same as the total volume of blood pumped?
items.correct: No. A rate must state the volume for each unit of time.
items.misconception: The rate is the total amount changed, whatever the time taken.
items.why: Students quote the number given in the question because it is the only volume they can see. Students should be able to use simple compound measures such as rate and carry out rate calculations for blood flow, giving the volume per unit of time.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which ventricle pumps blood to the lungs?
items.correct: The right ventricle.
items.misconception: The left ventricle pumps blood to the lungs.
items.why: Diagrams of the heart are drawn as though facing the patient, so the right side of the heart appears on the left of the page. The right ventricle pumps blood to the lungs where gas exchange takes place. The left ventricle pumps blood around the rest of the body.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do all arteries carry oxygenated blood?
items.correct: No. The pulmonary artery carries blood to the lungs for gas exchange.
items.misconception: All arteries carry blood that is rich in oxygen.
items.why: Students learn the useful rule that arteries carry blood away from the heart and then attach oxygen to it because most arteries do carry oxygenated blood. Knowledge of the blood vessels associated with the heart includes the pulmonary artery, which carries blood from the right ventricle to the lungs where gas exchange takes place.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Why is the wall of a capillary only one cell thick?
items.correct: So that substances can pass quickly between the blood and the tissues.
items.misconception: Capillaries have thick walls so that they can withstand the pressure of the blood.
items.why: Students apply the artery rule, that a strong wall resists pressure, to every vessel instead of matching structure to function. Students should be able to explain how the structure of these vessels relates to their functions: the capillary wall is one cell thick to allow exchange.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do red blood cells have a nucleus?
items.correct: No. They have no nucleus, which leaves more room for haemoglobin.
items.misconception: Red blood cells contain a nucleus like other animal cells.
items.why: Students learn that animal cells have a nucleus and apply the rule to every cell they are shown. Students should be able to recognise different types of blood cell in a photograph or diagram and explain how they are adapted to their functions: a red blood cell has no nucleus.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which part of the blood carries oxygen?
items.correct: The red blood cells, because they contain haemoglobin.
items.misconception: Plasma carries the oxygen around the body.
items.why: Plasma is described as the transport liquid of the blood, so students assume it carries everything, including oxygen. Blood is a tissue consisting of plasma, in which the red blood cells are suspended; the red blood cells are adapted to carry oxygen.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do stents lower the level of cholesterol in the blood?
items.correct: No. A stent is a device that holds the artery open.
items.misconception: Stents lower the level of cholesterol in the blood.
items.why: Both stents and statins are used for coronary heart disease, so students swap the mechanical device and the drug. Stents are used to keep the coronary arteries open, while statins are used to reduce blood cholesterol levels.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is an artificial heart a permanent replacement for a diseased heart?
items.correct: No. It is used while a patient waits for a transplant, or to allow the heart to rest.
items.misconception: An artificial heart is a permanent cure for heart failure.
items.why: The word 'artificial heart' suggests a complete replacement organ, like an artificial limb. Artificial hearts are occasionally used to keep patients alive whilst waiting for a heart transplant, or to allow the heart to rest as an aid to recovery.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does health mean being free from disease?
items.correct: No. Health is the state of physical and mental well-being.
items.misconception: Health means simply being free from disease.
items.why: Health is usually discussed in the context of illness, so students define it as the absence of illness rather than as well-being. Health is the state of physical and mental well-being, and other factors including diet, stress and life situations may have a profound effect on both physical and mental health.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is a study of 20 people enough to show that a substance is a risk factor?
items.correct: No. The sample is too small to represent the population reliably.
items.misconception: A small sample gives results that are as reliable as those from a large sample.
items.why: Students judge data by whether it shows a clear pattern rather than by how it was collected. Students should understand the principles of sampling as applied to scientific data, including epidemiological data.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are all cancers caused by lifestyle?
items.correct: No. There are also genetic risk factors for some cancers.
items.misconception: All cancers are caused by lifestyle factors such as smoking and diet.
items.why: Public health campaigns concentrate on lifestyle, so students assume every case must have a lifestyle cause. Scientists have identified lifestyle risk factors for various types of cancer. There are also genetic risk factors for some cancers.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Which blood vessels contain valves?
items.correct: Veins contain valves; arteries do not.
items.misconception: Arteries contain valves to stop the blood flowing backwards.
items.why: Valves are taught as the structure that keeps blood moving one way, so students give them to the vessel they think of as most important. Students should be able to explain how the structure of these vessels relates to their functions: valves are found in veins, where the blood is at low pressure.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Who bears the cost of non-communicable disease?
items.correct: The individual, and also the local community, the nation and the world.
items.misconception: Non-communicable disease costs affect only the person who is ill.
items.why: Non-communicable diseases cannot be passed on, so students assume their effects stop with the patient. Students should be able to discuss the human and financial cost of these non-communicable diseases to an individual, a local community, a nation or globally.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Where are the pacemaker cells found?
items.correct: In the right atrium of the heart.
items.misconception: The cells that set the resting heart rate are found in the left ventricle.
items.why: The left ventricle has the thickest muscle, so students assume it must be in charge of the beat. The natural resting heart rate is controlled by a group of cells located in the right atrium that act as a pacemaker.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How should the breakdown of starch by amylase be written?
items.correct: As a simple word equation, using the names of the substances: starch to sugars.
items.misconception: Digestion reactions have to be written as chemical symbol equations.
items.why: Students carry over the symbol equations and formulae they meet in chemistry lessons and assume the same is expected of them in biology. Students should be able to understand simple word equations, but no chemical symbol equations are required in this topic.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Biology (8461) specification; section 4.2.2 Animal Tissues, Organs & Systems
